picks.headline: AI-designed gene-editing enzymes expand the CRISPR toolbox
picks.excerpt: Scientists used the ESM Inverse Folding (ESM-IF1) AI protein-design model to generate synthetic TnpB gene-editing enzymes, dubbed SynTnpBs, starting from the known TnpB structure. In a study published in Science, several AI-designed variants outperformed the natural reference enzyme, reaching roughly 46-50% editing efficiency in human cells versus 28% for the original, expanding the compact genome-editing toolbox beyond CRISPR-Cas.
picks.rationale: AI-designed SynTnpB enzymes beating the natural reference (46-50% vs 28% editing efficiency), published in Science, is a concrete, high-credibility advance in AI-driven genome editing not in the science history.

picks.headline: AI tool predicts how DNA sequences switch on genes across different cell types
picks.excerpt: Martin Vingron's bioinformatics group at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics built Corgi (Context-aware Regulatory Genomics Inference), an AI tool that predicts how the genome behaves — which genes switch on and off — across different cell types. The work could sharpen efforts to model cell activity virtually, with applications in basic research and medicine.
picks.rationale: Corgi predicts cell-type-specific gene activity, a step toward virtual-cell modeling; distinct from the 07-26 DNA-binding card and directly useful to computational biologists.

picks.headline: The emerging field of cognitive brain-computer interfaces
picks.excerpt: A review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences (Mount Sinai) outlines a roadmap for the next generation of brain-computer interfaces aimed at cognitive disorders — depression, anxiety, PTSD, OCD — rather than motor function. Unlike today's movement- and speech-decoding BCIs, cognitive BCIs would rely on AI algorithms that decode dysfunctional brain states in real time and drive adaptive, closed-loop neurostimulation.
picks.rationale: A roadmap for AI-driven cognitive BCIs targeting depression, anxiety, PTSD and OCD via closed-loop neurostimulation — a fresh neuro/cognitive-science angle absent from the history.

picks.headline: Scientists built a camera that can track invisible particles in 3D
picks.excerpt: An ETH Zurich / EPFL team built PLATON, a particle detector that pairs a light-field (plenoptic) camera and single-photon avalanche-diode sensors with a Transformer-based neural network adapted from large language models to reconstruct particle paths in fast, detailed 3D from a single block of scintillator. Simulations suggest it could match or surpass today's best detectors while replacing millions of components, with potential spillover to sharper PET medical scans.
picks.rationale: PLATON pairs a light-field camera with a Transformer network borrowed from LLMs to reconstruct 3D particle tracks from one scintillator block — an AI-central particle-physics advance with PET-scan spillover, distinct from prior physics cards.
